description: We are Quantum Crew, a passionate team driven by robotics, software development, hardware prototyping, and space exploration. We combine coding, electronics, and creative problem-solving to turn bold ideas into working prototypes. Join us if you want a collaborative, high-energy squad ready to tackle tough challenges! We are looking for UI/UX designers, data scientists, video editors, and creative thinkers to complete our crew.
summary:
StormPulse is a web-based platform designed to transform NASA Earth observation data, particularly NISAR Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data, into actionable information for monitoring the impact of hurricanes and extreme weather events along the Mérida–Progreso corridor in Yucatán, Mexico.
The platform compares satellite observations from different dates to identify changes across this corridor, including flooding, coastal alterations, vegetation damage, and other surface changes associated with severe weather events. Instead of presenting complex scientific data, StormPulse translates these findings into an intuitive dashboard featuring interactive maps, recovery progress indicators, and a prioritized list of the five areas requiring the most attention. It also aims to estimate recovery timelines and integrate ground-based IoT sensors to validate satellite observations in critical locations.
StormPulse seeks to make SAR data more accessible and useful for emergency authorities, helping decision-makers understand the impact of extreme weather, prioritize resources, monitor recovery, and make informed decisions to protect communities and infrastructure along the Mérida–Progreso corridor.
details:
STORMPULSE is an operational decision-support application powered by an autonomous, predictive geospatial AI engine, initially deployed for post-hurricane flood response and emergency management across the karst terrain of the Mérida–Progreso corridor in Yucatán, Mexico, with a scalable architecture designed to expand its mapping coverage to additional regions in the future. Built directly in alignment with the "Dancing with the SARs" challenge for Civil Protection command centers and emergency response agencies, the application translates complex orbital predictions into an intuitive tactical interface that answers four critical operational questions at a glance: first, where recovery remains stalled, using a temporal slider and color-coded map that highlights dried zones in green—from which resources can be safely withdrawn—and stalled floodwaters in red; second, what the top five priorities are today, delivering a direct ranked list of critical sectors with exact recovery percentages and stagnation timelines to eliminate blind decision-making; third, how much longer the flooding will last, offering topography- and drainage-backed forecasts for road reopening and community return alongside simulations showing how additional water pumping cuts recovery timelines; and fourth, whether the satellite observation can be trusted, cross-referencing radar signatures in real time with terrain elevation, land cover, and accumulated precipitation to deliver a verified physical confidence indicator so commanders can sign deployment orders immediately without wasting hours sending crews to scout blindly.

Under the hood, the application is fed by a fully automated, multi-sensor orbital data pipeline that ingests Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery from NASA/ISRO NISAR (L-Band) and Copernicus Sentinel-1 (C-Band) to penetrate heavy tropical cloud cover, dense vegetation, and urban rooftops where optical satellites remain blind. The corridor is tessellated into standardized Uber H3 hexagonal grids, enriching each cell with NASA SRTM digital elevation models, terrain slope, accumulated precipitation, and ESA WorldCover land-use classifications. These inputs are processed by a LightGBM quantile regression ensemble—validated via blind historical backtesting against Hurricane Grace (2021) with a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 9.21 days—to predict recovery timelines under optimistic (P10), most-likely (P50), and worst-case (P90) scenarios. These predictions feed an exponential hydrological decay model to forecast daily recovery curves, which the application renders into color-coded GeoJSON maps, operational briefings, and high-resolution tactical dashboards highlighting priority sectors, mobility restoration timelines, and pump-deployment simulations.

By consuming 100% orbital radar data, the STORMPULSE application eliminates the cost, maintenance, and storm-damage vulnerability of physical IoT and water-level sensors, transforming raw satellite analytics into actionable morning briefings packaged in an isolated, lightweight, crash-proof architecture capable of running on standard local workstations without continuous cloud dependencies during grid outages. Ultimately, our goal is to bridge the gap between complex Earth observation intelligence and immediate field decisions during climate emergencies—equipping Civil Protection agencies in Yucatán with an operational, data-driven command application in the short term, and expanding its geospatial mapping coverage to broader territories, coastal municipalities, infrastructure operators, and risk-assessment organizations across hurricane-prone regions globally. To develop this application and its underlying AI engine, we utilized NASA/ISRO NISAR (L-Band SAR), Copernicus Sentinel-1 (C-Band SAR), NASA SRTM (Digital Elevation Model), ESA WorldCover, and Google Earth Engine (GEE) alongside Python 3, LightGBM (Quantile Regression), Scikit-Learn, NumPy, Pandas, PyArrow, Joblib, Uber H3 (spatial indexing), and Matplotlib, running on a virtualized Parrot OS (Linux) environment via Oracle VM VirtualBox with isolated Python virtual environments (venv), Git/GitHub, and QGIS/GeoJSON standards.
